title: York House to Gorhambury: the Instauration, the Fall, and the New Atlantis
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: York House, and the Boy Who Would Not Be Aristotle's

stops.name: York House, the Strand — birth
stops.campa: Francis Bacon is born at York House on the Strand, London seat of his father Sir Nicholas Bacon, Lord Keeper of the Great Seal to Elizabeth I. His mother, Anne Cooke Bacon, a scholar of Greek and a fierce reforming Protestant, will shape his mind before any tutor does. He is the youngest of Nicholas's second family, a small grave child in a household already at the hinge of the state: the Great Seal kept upstairs, statesmen at the table below. Law, learning, and the court share one roof over his cradle.
suggested_refs: York House on the Strand (site now Victoria Embankment Gardens; the York Watergate survives nearby)
sources: History of Parliament Online, 'BACON, Sir Francis (1561-1626)'

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge — entrance
stops.campa: At not quite twelve years old, Francis and his elder brother Anthony go up together to Trinity College, Cambridge, put under the tutelage of the Master, John Whitgift, future Archbishop of Canterbury. Francis is the youngest member of the college. He works with a gravity beyond his years and begins forming, in these rooms, the conviction he will carry his whole life: that the learning of the schools, built on Aristotle at second and third hand, is a barren inheritance, endlessly argued and never tested against nature herself.
suggested_refs: Trinity College, Cambridge, Great Court, where Bacon and his brother Anthony lodged

stops.name: Trinity College, Cambridge — the verdict against Aristotle
stops.campa: Before he leaves Cambridge at not yet fifteen, Bacon arrives, so his first biographer and chaplain William Rawley will record, at a judgment against the philosopher the whole university still swears by. He conceives a dislike of Aristotle's philosophy, Rawley writes, not for the worthlessness of the author but for the unfruitfulness of the way: a philosophy strong for disputations, barren of works for the benefit of man's life. It is the seed of everything after: the Advancement, the Novum Organum, a learning meant to bear fruit, not argument.
stops.quote: the unfruitfulness of the way; being a philosophy... only strong for disputations and contentions, but barren of the production of works for the benefit of the life of man
stops.quote_source: William Rawley, Life of the Honourable Author (1657 preface to Resuscitatio), recounting Bacon's own account
suggested_refs: Rawley's prefatory Life, the earliest biography of Bacon and the source of the Aristotle verdict
sources: William Rawley, Life of the Honourable Author (1657)

stops.name: Gray's Inn — admission
stops.campa: Back in London, Francis is admitted to Gray's Inn on the same day as his brother Anthony, entered de societate magistrorum on the books of the Inn of Court where his father kept chambers before him. He is meant for the law, the family trade, though his ambitions already reach further: not merely to plead causes but to reform the whole estate of knowledge. Within three months the Inn will lend him out again, across the Channel, into the household of a newly appointed ambassador to France.
suggested_refs: Gray's Inn Hall, Holborn, where Bacon kept chambers for the next fifty years

segments.name: The Paris Years, and a Cipher Conceived at Seventeen

stops.name: Paris — into the household of Sir Amias Paulet
stops.campa: In September, Queen Elizabeth having newly knighted Sir Amias Paulet and sent him as ambassador to the French court, Francis Bacon crosses to Paris in his train, put under his charge to learn the business of embassies. He carries dispatches to Walsingham, Burghley, Leicester, and the Queen herself, and begins the double education of a diplomat's clerk: the cipher and the code on one hand, the manners of princes on the other. Paris in these years is a court of plots and factions, the massacre of Saint Bartholomew still raw in memory.
suggested_refs: The English embassy in Paris under Sir Amias Paulet, 1576-1579
sources: History of Parliament Online, 'BACON, Sir Francis'

stops.name: Poitiers and the itinerant French court — civil law, and a cipher conceived
stops.campa: The embassy is itinerant, and Bacon follows the French court through its round of chateaux, Fontainebleau, Blois, Tours, Poitiers, Chenonceaux, carrying letters and watching the machinery of a foreign state at close range. At Poitiers he takes up civil law, the Roman-descended law of the continent, sharpening the comparative eye he will later turn on England's own courts. And here, not yet eighteen, he conceives the device that will outlast every office he ever holds: a cipher hiding one letter inside the shape of five, so any text at all may carry a second, secret text within it.
suggested_refs: Bacon's biliteral cipher, later published in De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623), conceived here at seventeen
sources: Elizabeth Wells Gallup, Concerning the Bi-Lateral Cypher of Francis Bacon

stops.name: Paris — the dream of Gorhambury in black mortar, and the father's death
stops.campa: Preparing to travel on into Italy, Bacon dreams one February night that Gorhambury, his father's house, stands plastered all over in black mortar. A fortnight later the news reaches Paris: on the twentieth, Sir Nicholas Bacon has died suddenly at York House, before completing the estate he meant to settle on his youngest son. Francis, not yet eighteen, abandons the Italian journey and sails home to a diminished inheritance, the law now not a choice but a necessity.
suggested_refs: Gorhambury, the house of the black-mortar dream, later Bacon's own retirement seat
sources: William Rawley, Life of the Honourable Author (1657)
History of Parliament Online, 'BACON, Sir Francis'

stops.name: Gray's Inn — the return, and the call to the law
stops.campa: Home in a country he has not lived in for three years, Bacon takes up residence at Gray's Inn and commits himself to the profession his father followed to the highest office in the land. The Continental polish, the civil law, the taste for cipher and secret method, all of it now bends toward the English bar, where a second son with no great fortune must make his own way by wit and patronage. He will be called to the bar within a few years, but the Essex years, not the law alone, will make him.
suggested_refs: Gray's Inn chambers, Bacon's professional home for the next four decades
sources: History of Parliament Online, 'BACON, Sir Francis'

segments.name: Essex, the Device, and a Province of All Knowledge

stops.name: Westminster — first seat in Parliament, for Bossiney
stops.campa: Bacon takes his first seat in the House of Commons, elected for the Cornish borough of Bossiney, beginning a parliamentary career that will run nearly four decades under three sovereigns. He is not yet twenty. Already he studies the House as he studies nature: a mechanism whose working parts, precedents and procedures, he means to master. He will sit for Melcombe, Taunton, Liverpool, and Middlesex in turn, gaining a reputation as one of the ablest speakers in England, admired even by those who distrust his ambition.
suggested_refs: Bossiney, Cornwall, the small borough of Bacon's first return
sources: History of Parliament Online, 'BACON, Sir Francis'

stops.name: Whitehall — the letter to Lord Burghley: 'all knowledge my province'
stops.campa: To his uncle by marriage, Lord Burghley, on whose favor his early career still depends, Bacon writes the letter that will be quoted longer than any office he ever holds. He confesses moderate ambitions in the state and vast ones in the mind: he means to purge the whole estate of learning of its two plagues, frivolous disputation and blind, credulous experiment, and bring in grounded, fruitful knowledge in their place. It is a young man's manifesto for the work of his whole life, decades before the Novum Organum gives it method.
stops.quote: I have taken all knowledge to be my province; and if I could purge it of two sorts of rovers, whereof the one with frivolous disputations, confutations, and verbosities, the other with blind experiments and auricular traditions and impostures, hath committed so many spoils, I hope I should bring in industrious observations, grounded conclusions, and profitable inventions and discoveries; the best state of that province.
suggested_refs: The 1592 letter to Burghley, Bacon's earliest statement of the Great Instauration

stops.name: Gray's Inn — the Gesta Grayorum, six speeches for the Prince of Purpoole
stops.campa: In the Christmas revels of Gray's Inn, the mock court of the Prince of Purpoole, Bacon writes six speeches of counsel for the Prince's councillors, urging in turn the study of philosophy, of arms, of eternal fame, of virtue, of the tillage of the mind, and of pastimes and sports: a masque of ambition disguised as entertainment. The same nights see the first recorded performance of a play called The Comedy of Errors in the crowded, overheated hall. Bacon works the revel like everything else: as an exercise in the government of minds.
suggested_refs: Gesta Grayorum, the printed record of the 1594 Gray's Inn revels, with Bacon's six speeches

stops.name: Twickenham Park — Essex's gift
stops.campa: Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, unable to win Bacon the Attorney's or Solicitor's place he has lobbied for, gives his friend and counselor instead the property at Twickenham Park, a riverside house and grounds upstream of London, in compensation for a service patronage alone could not reward. Bacon keeps it for years, walking the gardens between law terms, testing early thoughts on soils and orchards there, and sells it in the end for eighteen hundred pounds. It is the clearest sign yet of how much the two men owe each other, and of how little that debt will finally protect either of them.
suggested_refs: Twickenham Park on the Thames, Essex's gift to Bacon
sources: History of Parliament Online, 'BACON, Sir Francis'

stops.name: Gray's Inn — the Essays, and the Walks planted
stops.campa: Bacon publishes the first slim Essays, ten of them, terse counsel on studies, discourse, honor, and negotiation, the beginning of a book he will keep enlarging the rest of his life. The same year he takes the Gray's Inn garden in hand, laying out the Walks with elms and raised mounts, a design so lasting that Londoners still stroll it centuries on. Words for the mind and trees for the eye, planted in the same season: already the man who will one day found Salomon's House, tending letters and gardens both as forms of one instauration.
suggested_refs: The Gray's Inn Walks, Bacon's own garden design, still standing in Holborn
sources: gardenvisit.com, 'London Parks and Gardens 1907, Gray's Inn Gardens'

stops.name: London — arrested for debt
stops.campa: Bacon's debts catch up with him: on the twenty-third of September he is arrested for debt and held, not long, in a sponging house in the City, an embarrassment to a rising counsel and Queen's servant. Essex, ever generous where his own fortunes allow, helps settle the matter, deepening still further the weight of favor Bacon owes him. The man who will one day hold the Great Seal of England cannot yet keep his own accounts in order, a fault that will follow him, in one form or another, to the very end of his public life.
suggested_refs: Bacon's lifelong debts, a thread running from this 1598 arrest to the tens of thousands owed at his death

stops.name: Essex House — the Rebellion
stops.campa: Robert Devereux, ruined in fortune and standing after his failed Irish command, gathers armed followers at Essex House and marches them into the City, hoping to raise the citizens against the councillors he blames for his fall. The City does not rise. Within hours the rebellion collapses and Essex surrenders. Bacon, who has warned his friend and patron for years against exactly this kind of rashness, and who has already begun distancing himself in letters to Robert Cecil, watches the ruin of a man he owes almost everything, from across a widening gulf.
suggested_refs: Essex House on the Strand, the rebellion's staging ground

stops.name: Westminster Hall — the trial
stops.campa: At the trial in Westminster Hall, Bacon stands among the Crown's counsel prosecuting the earl who made his career possible, arguing treason against the friend who gave him Twickenham Park and every start he never got from the Queen. It is the disagreeable task, discharged, contemporaries will say, with more zeal than the office strictly required. Essex and Southampton are convicted; only Essex is condemned to die. Bacon's own voice helped seal it, and the fact will follow him into every account he writes of his own life hereafter.
suggested_refs: The 1601 treason trial record, and Bacon's own later Declaration of the Practises and Treasons
sources: Royal Collection Trust, 'A Declaration of the practices and treasons...'

stops.name: The Tower of London — the execution
stops.campa: On the green within the Tower, spared the crowd of Tower Hill by the Queen's own mercy, Robert Devereux is beheaded, still protesting his loyalty to her person even as he dies a traitor to her state. Bacon does not attend, but will spend the rest of his life answering for the part he played in bringing the earl here: counselor turned prosecutor, friend who chose the Crown. Elizabeth herself, it is said, never fully recovers her old brightness after this execution; within two years she too will be dead.
suggested_refs: The Tower of London's inner court, where Essex was executed away from the public crowd

stops.name: London — the Apologie published
stops.campa: Three years on, with a new king on the throne and old wounds unhealed, Bacon publishes his Apologie, in Certaine Imputations Concerning the Late Earle of Essex: a careful, self-justifying account of every service and every warning given his fallen patron, and of why the prosecution was duty and not betrayal. It persuades some and not others. The charge of ingratitude will be repeated against him for the rest of his career and long after, a shadow not even the Novum Organum will fully dispel.
suggested_refs: Francis Bacon, Apologie, in Certaine Imputations Concerning the Late Earle of Essex (1604)

segments.name: Knighthood, Marriage, and the Advancement of Learning

stops.name: Whitehall — knighted by the new king
stops.campa: With the accession of James VI of Scotland as James I of England, three hundred gentlemen are knighted in a single sweeping ceremony to mark the new reign, and Bacon is one of them, his old service to Elizabeth's Essex now safely behind a king who owes him nothing and everything is still to be won. He sets himself at once to court the new sovereign's favor with treatises and flattery both, reading in James's own pedantic learning an opening no other client at court can match.
suggested_refs: The mass knighting of July 1603, marking James I's accession

stops.name: London — The Advancement of Learning published
stops.campa: Bacon publishes The Advancement of Learning, dedicated to King James: a survey of the whole map of human knowledge and of everywhere it has been neglected, corrupted, or falsely finished before its time. It is the first public sketch of the project that will occupy the rest of his life, not a single book of philosophy but an instauration, a rebuilding of learning from its foundations, so knowledge might finally bear fruit for the relief of man's estate rather than merely furnish disputation for the schools.
suggested_refs: The Advancement of Learning (1605), the first English statement of the Great Instauration

stops.name: Marylebone Chapel — marriage to Alice Barnham
stops.campa: At Marylebone Chapel, in the fields north of London, Bacon marries Alice Barnham, daughter of a London alderman and not yet fourteen. He comes clad from top to toe in purple, and the cloth of silver and gold he orders for them both draws so deep into her portion that the court letter-writers make a joke of it. It is a marriage of property and connection more than passion. The couple will have no children, and in a will drawn in bitterness in 1625 Bacon will revoke every gift and settlement made to her, leaving her, in his own cold phrase, to her right only.
suggested_refs: Marylebone Chapel, the second parish church at the north end of Marylebone High Street (demolished; the site is now a public garden), where Bacon married in 1606

stops.name: Westminster — Solicitor General
stops.campa: After a decade of disappointed applications under Elizabeth, Bacon is at last appointed Solicitor General, the office he had twice failed to win before, now granted under a king more susceptible to his particular blend of learning, flattery, and legal craft. It is the true beginning of the second half of his career: the climb through the great offices of the Crown that will carry him, within little more than a decade, to the highest civil office in the land, and not much later, to the fastest fall of any Lord Chancellor in English history.
suggested_refs: The office of Solicitor General, Bacon's first great Crown appointment

stops.name: Westminster — Attorney General
stops.campa: Bacon is made Attorney General, the Crown's chief law officer, a post he pursues with the same patient ambition brought to every rung below it. He is now the most powerful lawyer in England after the judges themselves, and will use the place to draw closer still to the king's favorites, first Somerset and then the young Buckingham, whose rise he helps engineer and whose favor will carry him, in turn, to the woolsack.
suggested_refs: The office of Attorney General under James I, Bacon's post from 1613 to 1617

segments.name: The Hidden Work: the Fama and the Confessio

stops.name: Kassel — the Fama Fraternitatis circulates
stops.campa: In the German lands, a strange manifesto begins to circulate in manuscript and then in print at Kassel: the Fama Fraternitatis, announcing to all Europe a hidden brotherhood of the Rosy Cross, founded generations before by one Christian Rosenkreuz, keepers of a secret natural philosophy and a promise of universal reformation. A persistent tradition, never proved and never quite silenced, holds that the guiding hand, even the pen, behind the Rosicrucian manifestos was Bacon's own, working through continental intermediaries to seed abroad the same instauration he was building at home in English.
suggested_refs: The Fama Fraternitatis (Kassel, 1614), founding text of the Rosicrucian tradition
sources: Francis Bacon Society, 'Bacon, Shakespeare, and the Rosicrucians'

stops.name: Kassel — the Confessio Fraternitatis follows
stops.campa: A second manifesto follows, the Confessio Fraternitatis, sharpening the first's promise into a fuller creed: the corrupt learning of the schools must fall, a new philosophy of nature and light is coming, and the brotherhood watches unseen across Europe for the moment to reveal itself. Those in the tradition who name Bacon its hidden architect point to the shared vocabulary of instauration and universal reform, the shared contempt for Aristotle's schoolmen, and the shared dream of a college of natural philosophers working in secret toward the public good, the dream that surfaces, a decade on, as Salomon's House.
suggested_refs: The Confessio Fraternitatis (1615), and its echo in the language of Bacon's own Instauratio Magna
sources: Francis Bacon Society, 'Bacon, Shakespeare, and the Rosicrucians'

segments.name: Under the Seal: Somerset, Lord Keeper, and the Viscountcy

stops.name: Westminster Hall — the prosecution of Somerset and Frances Howard
stops.campa: As Attorney General, Bacon leads the Crown's prosecution of Robert Carr, Earl of Somerset, and his wife Frances Howard for the poisoning murder of Sir Thomas Overbury, a scandal reaching into the king's own bedchamber favorites. Both are convicted; both are, in the end, quietly pardoned by a king unwilling to lose a former favorite entirely to the block. Bacon prosecutes with his usual command of evidence and argument, careful, as ever, never to let the trail of guilt climb high enough to touch the throne itself.
suggested_refs: The 1616 Overbury murder trial, Westminster Hall

stops.name: York House — Lord Keeper of the Great Seal
stops.campa: James I makes Bacon Lord Keeper of the Great Seal, the very office his father Sir Nicholas held for twenty years, and installs him, fittingly, at York House on the Strand: the house of his birth, now the house of his highest office. For one month, in the king's absence in Scotland, Bacon even serves as sole regent of England, a commoner's son briefly governing the whole kingdom in all but name.
suggested_refs: York House, the Strand: birthplace and, now, the Lord Keeper's official residence

stops.name: York House — Lord Chancellor, and Baron Verulam
stops.campa: Bacon is raised to Lord Chancellor, the highest judicial office in England, and within the year created Baron Verulam, taking his title from the Roman town beside his own Gorhambury. He has now climbed every rung his father climbed, and higher: son and father alike have held the Great Seal, but only Francis wears a peer's coronet for it. He keeps a magnificence at York House his income cannot support, entertaining lavishly, sitting for the portraits of a man who has arrived exactly where his letters to Burghley, decades before, said he meant to go.
suggested_refs: The barony of Verulam, named for the Roman town beside Gorhambury

stops.name: London — the Instauratio Magna and the Novum Organum
stops.campa: Bacon publishes the Novum Organum, the New Instrument, as the second part of his unfinished Instauratio Magna, the Great Instauration of the sciences. Its title page shows a ship sailing out between the Pillars of Hercules into open ocean, over the motto Plus Ultra, further beyond, the ancient limit of knowledge broken. Within, he lays out the four Idols that darken the human mind, of the Tribe, the Cave, the Marketplace, and the Theatre, and the method of induction that must replace them: patient, structured experiment, the only road by which nature yields her secrets and knowledge becomes, at last, power.
stops.quote: There are four classes of Idols which beset men's minds. To these for distinction's sake I have assigned names, calling the first class Idols of the Tribe; the second, Idols of the Cave; the third, Idols of the Market-place; the fourth, Idols of the Theatre.
stops.quote_source: Novum Organum, Book I, Aphorism XXXIX (1620), Spedding translation
suggested_refs: The Instauratio Magna frontispiece: a ship passing the Pillars of Hercules, motto Plus Ultra
sources: fs.blog, 'Francis Bacon and the Four Idols of the Mind'

stops.name: Westminster — created Viscount St Alban
stops.campa: At the height of his fortune, five days after his sixtieth birthday, Bacon is created Viscount St Alban, the last and highest honor the king will ever grant him. He has, in one generation, out-titled his own father; he sits as Lord Chancellor with a peerage, a great house, a new philosophy half-published, and creditors he has long since stopped trying to count. Within ten weeks a parliamentary committee will open the inquiry that ends all of it, and he does not yet see it coming.
suggested_refs: The title Viscount St Alban, held only from January to the impeachment that spring

stops.name: Westminster — the charges of Chancery bribery
stops.campa: A parliamentary committee investigating abuses in the courts brings forward specific charges against the Lord Chancellor: suitors in Chancery, it is alleged, have paid him gifts and fees while their cases were still pending before him. His old enemy Sir Edward Coke, restored to influence and never forgiving Bacon his years of preferment, helps drive the inquiry forward. Twenty-three counts accumulate. Bacon, ill and slow to grasp how fast the ground is shifting, at first tries to answer point by point; the House will not be satisfied with answers.
suggested_refs: The 1621 parliamentary inquiry into Chancery abuses, the Third Parliament of James I

stops.name: The House of Lords — the confession
stops.campa: Learning that the king himself now expects a confession, Bacon submits. Asked by a committee of the Lords whether the written acknowledgment sent to them is truly his own, he answers in words that will outlive the charges themselves: it is his act, his hand, his heart, and he begs their mercy for a broken reed. He does not deny receiving gifts from litigants; he denies only that any gift ever swayed a judgment, a distinction the House does not trouble to weigh very finely.
stops.quote: My lords, it is my act, my hand, and my heart; I beseech your lordships to be merciful to a broken reed.
stops.quote_source: Confession before the House of Lords committee, 1621
suggested_refs: The written confession submitted to the House of Lords, spring 1621

stops.name: The Tower of London — the sentence
stops.campa: The Lords pronounce sentence: a fine of forty thousand pounds, imprisonment in the Tower during the king's pleasure, incapacity ever again to hold office or sit in Parliament, and banishment from within twelve miles of the court. Bacon is committed to the Tower and remains there some three or four days before the king, never intending the full severity of a sentence he had all but engineered a milder version of behind the scenes, orders his release. The fine, too, will never be collected. The public ruin, unlike the private one, is complete and permanent.
suggested_refs: The Tower of London, Bacon's brief 1621 imprisonment

stops.name: Gorhambury — the retirement begins
stops.campa: Stripped of office, barred from Parliament and from the verge of the court, Bacon withdraws to Gorhambury, his father's old house outside St Albans, to what will become the last, and by his own later judgment the most productive, five years of his life. Freed of the law's business and the endless suits of Chancery, he turns his whole remaining strength to the unfinished work of the Instauration: histories, natural philosophy, the utopia long carried unwritten in his mind. Disgrace, he tells a friend, has at least given him leisure he could never have bought as Chancellor.
suggested_refs: Old Gorhambury House, Bacon's retirement and the site of his last five years' writing

segments.name: Gorhambury, the New Atlantis, and the Phoenix of Highgate

stops.name: Gorhambury — The History of the Reign of King Henry VII
stops.campa: At Gorhambury, within a year of his fall, Bacon completes The History of the Reign of King Henry VII, a study of the founder of the Tudor line written with the same cool analytic eye once turned on nature and the law: a king's use of parliament, coinage, and marriage alliance laid open like the workings of a machine. It is one of the earliest works of English history to treat statecraft as a subject of empirical study rather than moral fable, disgrace turned, as he intended, into instauration.
suggested_refs: The History of the Reign of King Henry VII (1622), written in the first year of retirement

stops.name: Gorhambury — De Augmentis Scientiarum, the cipher set out in full
stops.campa: Bacon publishes De Augmentis Scientiarum, a vastly enlarged Latin edition of The Advancement of Learning, and in it at last sets out in full, with plates of the alphabet, the biliteral cipher conceived as a boy of seventeen in Paris: letters written in one of two nearly identical type-forms, five characters standing for one, so an entirely innocent-looking text can carry a second, hidden message inside its very shape. It is the plainest evidence the canon offers that Bacon spent a lifetime writing in more than one register at once, a habit later readers will chase into every line he ever signed, and many he did not.
suggested_refs: The biliteral cipher plate in De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623), the alphabet of two almost-identical types

stops.name: London — the First Folio, and the tradition of the hidden author
stops.campa: In London, the printers Jaggard and Blount issue the First Folio of Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies, gathering thirty-six plays between covers for the first time. A tradition that will only grow over the centuries holds that the true author behind the plays, or at least a hidden hand within this very edition, is Bacon himself, his biliteral cipher and other devices worked into the Folio's dedicatory verses, ornaments, and page numbers, encoding a secret history and a philosopher's authorship never publicly claimed. The claim is never proved; within the tradition, it is never abandoned either.
suggested_refs: The First Folio (1623), central text of the Baconian cipher-hunters
sources: Francis Bacon Society, 'Bacon, Shakespeare, and the Rosicrucians'
Academia.edu, "Francis Bacon's Rosicrucian De Augmentis Scientiarum (1623) & the Key to His Biliteral Cipher"

stops.name: Gorhambury — the King's pardon under the Great Seal
stops.campa: The king grants Bacon a full pardon under the Great Seal, restoring him formally in blood and estate though never to office, while Parliament briefly and unsuccessfully entertains restoring his seat as well. It is as much vindication as the age will offer him: the fine forgiven in substance if not in name, the sentence's harshest teeth drawn, while the verdict itself, and the incapacity for public life, stand unrepealed. He accepts it for what it is, partial mercy, and returns to his papers.
suggested_refs: The 1624 pardon under the Great Seal

stops.name: Gorhambury — the New Atlantis, and Salomon's House
stops.campa: In these Gorhambury years Bacon writes, and leaves unfinished, the New Atlantis: a ship's company cast up on the undiscovered island of Bensalem, where they find a Christian kingdom ruled not by kings' whims but by the ordered pursuit of nature's secrets, gathered in a great foundation called Salomon's House. There the fellows sweep the created world for knowledge, caves for preserving bodies, towers for weather and flight, engines for sound and light, all bent to one declared end. It is the clearest picture Bacon draws of the Instauration finished, a college for a knowledge no single mind could hold alone.
stops.quote: The end of our foundation is the knowledge of causes, and secret motions of things; and the enlarging of the bounds of human empire, to the effecting of all things possible.
stops.quote_source: New Atlantis (written c. 1624, published posthumously 1627), the words of the Father of Salomon's House
suggested_refs: Salomon's House, the fictional foundation of New Atlantis, the acknowledged model for the 'invisible college' and, through it, the Royal Society
sources: The Square Magazine, "Sir Francis Bacon and Salomon's House"

stops.name: Highgate Hill — the snow, and the hen
stops.campa: Riding toward Highgate with his physician Dr Witherborne on a day of falling snow, Bacon falls to wondering, as he has wondered about a hundred things before, whether flesh might be preserved in snow as well as in salt. He will not let the question wait for a study. They stop at a poor woman's cottage at the foot of the hill, buy a hen, have it drawn, and stuff the carcass with snow, Bacon himself helping with his own hands. The chill of the experiment passes at once into his own body; he cannot make it back to his lodgings that night.
stops.quote: I was likely to have had the fortune of Caius Plinius the elder, who lost his life by trying an experiment about the burning of Mount Vesuvius; for I was also desirous to try an experiment or two touching the conservation and induration of bodies.
stops.quote_source: Bacon's last letter, to Lord Arundel, written from Arundel House at Highgate, April 1626
suggested_refs: The frozen hen of Highgate, and the ghost said still to haunt Pond Square, featherless and shrieking
sources: the-microbiologist.com, 'Ice, ice, maybe? Francis Bacon and frozen meat'

stops.name: Arundel House, Highgate — the death
stops.campa: Bacon is carried to the Earl of Arundel's own house at Highgate, put to bed in a room warmed with a pan but damp from a year's disuse. That bed, Aubrey says, kills him: within two or three days the cold turns to what his own age calls a defluxion, a suffocating catarrh settling on the chest, and he dies in the house on the ninth of April, not yet sixty-six. His debts run past twenty-two thousand pounds, far beyond anything the estate can meet; the philosopher of the Instauration dies, as he had long lived, in the red.
suggested_refs: Arundel House at Highgate (since demolished), where Bacon died
sources: hauntedpalaceblog.com, 'The Strange Case of Sir Francis Bacon and the Frozen Chicken'

stops.name: St Michael's Church, St Albans — the burial, and the seated monument
stops.campa: He is buried, as he asked, at St Michael's Church in St Albans, near his mother, in the town that takes its name from the Roman Verulamium beside which he had taken his own title. Years later his friend and former secretary Sir Thomas Meautys pays for a monument: a life-sized figure seated in an armchair, head resting on one hand, a strangely modern pose of thought rather than triumph. The Latin beneath calls him, in the era's own measure, the light of science and the law of eloquence, and asks that his compounded parts now be dissolved.
stops.quote: Francis Bacon... of Science the Light, of Eloquence the Law, sat thus. Who after all Natural Wisdom and Secret of Civil Life he had unfolded, Nature's law fulfilled: let compounds be dissolved.
stops.quote_source: Latin epitaph on the monument at St Michael's Church, St Albans (translated)
